William Henry Harrison (February 9, 1773 – April 4, 1841) was the ninth president of the United States from March to April 1841. He died 31 days into his term, making him the shortest serving president and the first president to die in office.

The last chapter of William Henry Harrison was written long after the fame. Immediately after his death, Vice President John Tyler took over, ending the constitutional crisis that had been triggered by the question of presidential succession in the U.S. A member of the Harrison family of Virginia, he was a son of Benjamin Harrison V, a Founding Father, and the father of John Scott Harrison, the only son and father of two presidents of the United States.

The whole life of William Henry Harrison reads like a single decision repeated. In 1794, he participated in the Battle of Fallen Timbers, an American military victory that ended the Northwest Indian War. In 1811, he led a military force against Tecumseh's confederacy at the Battle of Tippecanoe, for which he earned the nickname "Old Tippecanoe".

Between the birth and the legend of William Henry Harrison lie the years that actually decide it. He was promoted to major general in the Army during the War of 1812, and led American infantry and cavalry to victory at the Battle of the Thames in Upper Canada. Harrison's political career began in 1798, with an appointment as secretary of the Northwest Territory.

The reputation of William Henry Harrison was built in the middle, not at the edges. In 1799, he was elected as the territory's non-voting delegate in the U.S. He became governor of the newly established Indiana Territory in 1801 and, through multiple treaties with American Indian tribes, he acquired millions of acres for the nation.

Somebody like William Henry Harrison should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. After the War of 1812, he moved to Ohio where, in 1816, he was elected to represent the state's 1st district in the House. Senate, though his Senate term was cut short by his appointment as minister plenipotentiary to Gran Colombia in 1828.

The life of William Henry Harrison begins far from where the story usually starts. Harrison returned to private life in Ohio until he was one of four Whig Party nominees in the 1836 U.S. presidential election, which he lost to Democrat Martin Van Buren. In the 1840 presidential election, the party nominated him again, with John Tyler as his running mate, under the campaign slogan "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too", and Harrison defeated Van Buren.

William Henry Harrison was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Just three weeks after his inauguration, Harrison fell ill and died days later. After resolution of an ambiguity in the constitution regarding succession, Tyler became president.

To understand where William Henry Harrison ended up, start with where William Henry Harrison began. He is typically ranked in the bottom quartile of historical presidential rankings due to the brevity of his tenure, though for the same reason he, as well as James A. William Henry Harrison was the seventh and youngest child of Benjamin Harrison V and Elizabeth (Bassett) Harrison.

The road from the beginning to the peak of William Henry Harrison ran through years nobody filmed. Born on February 9, 1773, at Berkeley Plantation, the home of the Harrison family of Virginia on the James River in Charles City County, he became the last United States president not born as an American citizen. The Harrisons were a prominent political family of English descent whose ancestors had been in Virginia since the 1630s.

Each stage of the life of William Henry Harrison made the next stage possible. His father was a Virginia planter, who served as a delegate to the Continental Congress and who signed the Declaration of Independence. His father also served in the Virginia legislature and as the fifth governor of Virginia (1781–1784) in the years during and after the American Revolutionary War.

The people who knew William Henry Harrison young describe someone already restless. Harrison's older brother Carter Bassett Harrison represented Virginia in the House of Representatives (1793–1799). William Henry often referred to himself as a "child of the revolution", as indeed he was, having grown up in a home just 30 mi (48 km) from where Washington won the war against the British in the Battle of Yorktown.

What William Henry Harrison built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Harrison was tutored at home until age 14 when he attended Hampden–Sydney College, a Presbyterian college in Hampden Sydney, Virginia. He studied there for three years, receiving a classical education that included Latin, Greek, French, logic, and debate.

By the time William Henry Harrison reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. His Episcopalian father removed him from the college, possibly for religious reasons, and after brief stays at an academy in Southampton County, Virginia, and with his elder brother Benjamin Harrison VI in Richmond, he went to Philadelphia in 1790. His father died in the spring of 1791, and he was placed in the care of Robert Morris, a close family friend in Philadelphia.

The rise of William Henry Harrison was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. While at Penn, he studied with Benjamin Rush, a Founding Father of the United States, a Penn professor of chemistry and medicine, and a doctor, and William Shippen Sr. William Harrison's older brother inherited their father's money, so William lacked the funds for his further medical schooling, which he had also discovered he did not prefer.

Setbacks came early for William Henry Harrison, and the response to them is the real story. He withdrew from Penn, although school archives record him as a "non-graduate alumnus of Penn's medical school class of 1793". With the influence of his father's friend, Governor Henry Lee III, he embarked upon a military career.

The legacy of William Henry Harrison outlived the circumstances that produced it. On August 16, 1791, within 24 hours of meeting Lee, William Harrison, age 18, was commissioned as an ensign in the United States Army and assigned to the First American Regiment. He was initially assigned to Fort Washington, Cincinnati in the Northwest Territory where the army was engaged in the ongoing Northwest Indian War.

Few lives travel as far as that of William Henry Harrison, and the distance is the point. Freehling says that young Harrison, in his first military act, rounded up about eighty thrill-seekers and troublemakers off Philadelphia's streets, talked them into signing enlistment papers, and marched them to Fort Washington. Harrison was promoted to lieutenant after Major General "Mad Anthony" Wayne took command of the western army in 1792, after a disastrous defeat under Arthur St.

The childhood of William Henry Harrison contains the adult in small print. In 1793, he became Wayne's aide-de-camp and acquired the skills to command an army on the frontier; he participated in Wayne's decisive victory at the Battle of Fallen Timbers on August 20, 1794, which ended the Northwest Indian War. Under the terms of the treaty, a coalition of Indians ceded a portion of their lands to the federal government, opening two-thirds of Ohio to settlement.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of William Henry Harrison — in that order. At his mother's death in 1793, Harrison inherited a portion of his family's Virginia estate, including approximately 3,000 acres (12 km2) of land and some slaves. He was serving in the Army at the time and sold the land to his brother.

The turning point in the life of William Henry Harrison looked like a failure at the time. Harrison was promoted to captain in May 1797 and resigned from the Army on June 1, 1798. Harrison met Anna Tuthill Symmes of North Bend, Ohio in 1795 when he was 22.

Every biography of William Henry Harrison has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. She was a daughter of Anna Tuthill and Judge John Cleves Symmes, who served as a colonel in the Revolutionary War and as a representative to the Congress of the Confederation. Harrison asked the judge for permission to marry Anna but was refused, so the couple waited until Symmes left on business.

The education of William Henry Harrison happened mostly outside any school. They then eloped and were married on November 25, 1795, at the North Bend home of Stephen Wood, treasurer of the Northwest Territory. Judge Symmes confronted him two weeks later at a farewell dinner for General Wayne, sternly demanding to know how he intended to support a family.

What William Henry Harrison wanted at the start and what William Henry Harrison got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. The match was advantageous for Harrison, as he eventually exploited his father-in-law's connections with land speculators, which facilitated his departure from the army. Anna was frequently in poor health during their marriage, primarily because of her many pregnancies, yet she outlived William by 23 years, dying on February 25, 1864, at 88.

The defining trait of William Henry Harrison was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Janken, in his biography of Walter Francis White, claims that Harrison had six children by an enslaved African-American woman named Dilsia and, before running for president, gave four of them to a brother to avoid scandal. In her 2012 biography of Harrison, author Gail Collins describes this as an unlikely story, although White believed it to be true.

Those who met William Henry Harrison at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Harrison began his political career when he temporarily resigned from the military on June 1, 1798, and campaigned among his friends and family for a post in the Northwest Territorial government. His close friend Timothy Pickering was serving as Secretary of State, and along with Judge Symmes's influence, he was recommended to replace Winthrop Sargent, the outgoing territorial secretary.

The private years of William Henry Harrison explain the public decades better than any speech. The work of recording the activities of the territory was tedious, and he soon became bored, and sought a position in the U.S. Harrison had many friends in the Eastern aristocracy and quickly gained a reputation among them as a frontier leader.

The family William Henry Harrison came from matters more than the legends admit. Congress had legislated a territorial policy that led to high land costs, a primary concern for settlers in the Territory; Harrison became their champion to lower those prices. The Northwest Territory's population reached a sufficient number to have a congressional delegate in October 1799, and Harrison ran for election.

The first real success of William Henry Harrison arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Clair Jr. to become the Northwest Territory's first congressional delegate in 1798 at age 26, and served in the Sixth United States Congress from March 4, 1799, to May 14, 1800. He had no authority to vote on legislative bills, but he was permitted to serve on a committee, to submit legislation, and to engage in debate.

The last chapter of William Henry Harrison was written long after the fame. He became chairman of the Committee on Public Lands and promoted the Land Act of 1800, which made it easier to buy Northwest Territory land in smaller tracts at a lower cost. Freeholders were permitted to buy smaller lots with a down payment of only five percent, and this became an important factor in the Territory's rapid population growth.

The whole life of William Henry Harrison reads like a single decision repeated. Harrison was also instrumental in arranging the division of the Territory into two sections. The eastern section continued to be known as the Northwest Territory and included present-day Ohio and eastern Michigan; the western section was named the Indiana Territory and included present-day Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, a portion of western Michigan, and an eastern portion of Minnesota.

Between the birth and the legend of William Henry Harrison lie the years that actually decide it. On May 13, 1800, President John Adams appointed Harrison as the governor of the Indiana Territory, based on his ties to the west and his apparent neutral political stances. His governorship was confirmed by the Senate and he resigned from Congress to become the first Indiana territorial governor in 1801.

The reputation of William Henry Harrison was built in the middle, not at the edges. Harrison began his duties on January 10, 1801, at Vincennes, the capital of the Indiana Territory. Presidents Thomas Jefferson and James Madison were members of the Democratic-Republican Party, and they reappointed him as governor in 1803, 1806, and 1809.
